q: (R)-2-Ethyl-2-methyloxirane is treated with CH3OH and a catalytic amount of H2SO4. What is the major product?
h: Acid sets the regiochemistry (which carbon); the back-side attack sets the configuration at that carbon.
w: Under acid, methanol attacks the tertiary carbon of the protonated epoxide. The attack is back-side, opposite the leaving oxygen (the ring is still bonded, so no free carbocation forms), so that stereocenter is inverted. Ranking the product carbon: OCH3 > CH2OH > CH2CH3 > CH3; with inversion this gives (S)-2-methoxy-2-methylbutan-1-ol (checked with CIP software).
x: Retention of configuration would need front-side attack; acid-catalyzed epoxide opening is back-side even at a tertiary carbon.
This is the product of attack at the CH<sub>2</sub> carbon, the regiochemistry for basic conditions (e.g. NaOCH<sub>3</sub>).
The ring oxygen is still bonded when methanol attacks, so there is no free planar carbocation and no racemization.

q: Cyclohexene oxide reacts with HBr to give 2-bromocyclohexan-1-ol. Which describes the product in the chair conformation in which it is first formed?
h: Bromide attacks anti to the C–O bond. In a half-chair, which direction is anti to the epoxide oxygen?
w: Bromide attacks the protonated epoxide from the side opposite the oxygen (anti opening). In the cyclohexane ring that path keeps the nucleophile and the leaving oxygen on a common axis, so the new C–Br bond and the C–OH bond are both axial on opposite faces: the product forms trans-diaxial. It then ring-flips to the more stable diequatorial chair, but it stays trans.
x: The diequatorial chair is the more stable conformer reached after a ring flip; it is not the chair formed directly by anti opening.
Anti (back-side) opening always puts Br and OH on opposite faces, so the product is trans, not cis.
A cis product would need syn delivery of Br; epoxide opening is anti, giving the trans isomer.

q: Cyclohexene oxide is treated with (1) NaN<sub>3</sub> in aqueous ethanol, then (2) LiAlH<sub>4</sub>, then (3) H<sub>2</sub>O. What is the product (racemic; one enantiomer drawn)?
h: Azide is a strong nucleophile. Track the stereochemistry of the ring opening, then ask what LiAlH<sub>4</sub> does to an azide.
w: Azide opens the epoxide by SN2 from the face opposite the oxygen, giving trans-2-azidocyclohexan-1-ol. LiAlH4 reduces the azide (–N3) to a primary amine (–NH2) without touching the stereocenters. Product: trans-2-aminocyclohexan-1-ol.
x: This is the cis isomer; S<sub>N</sub>2 opening of the epoxide is anti, so N and O end up trans.
This is the intermediate after step 1; LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduces the azide to an amine.
Azide is far more nucleophilic than water, so the epoxide is opened by N<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>, not hydrolyzed to the diol.

q: What is the major product of this reaction?
h: Hydride from LiAlH<sub>4</sub> is a strong nucleophile. Where does a strong nucleophile open an epoxide?
w: Hydride (from AlH4−) opens the epoxide by SN2 at the less hindered secondary carbon. The oxygen stays on the tertiary carbon, and acid workup protonates it: 1-methylcyclohexan-1-ol.
x: This would need hydride to attack the tertiary carbon, which is too hindered for S<sub>N</sub>2.
LiAlH<sub>4</sub> adds one H; it does not add a second oxygen, so no diol forms.
LiAlH<sub>4</sub> opens the ring to an alcohol; it does not remove the oxygen to regenerate the alkene.

q: What is the product after phenylmagnesium bromide reacts with oxirane (ethylene oxide) and the mixture is worked up with aqueous acid?
h: The Grignard carbon bonds to a ring carbon; the oxygen ends up two carbons away.
w: The aryl carbanion attacks one CH2 of oxirane by SN2, opening the strained ring. Workup protonates the alkoxide. The phenyl group gains a two-carbon chain ending in OH: 2-phenylethan-1-ol. Grignard + oxirane adds two carbons, with the OH on the second carbon.
x: 1-Phenylethanol would form from PhMgBr + acetaldehyde (or CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr + benzaldehyde), not from oxirane.
Benzyl alcohol has only one carbon between ring and OH; it is the product with formaldehyde, which adds one carbon.
Oxirane adds two carbons, not three; three carbons would need oxetane.

q: Which reagents give the alcohol shown as the major product?
h: For each pair, put the Grignard carbon on the less hindered epoxide carbon and draw what results.
w: Grignard reagents open epoxides at the less hindered carbon. Phenyl attacks the CH2 of 2-methyloxirane, and the O stays on the CH(CH3) carbon: C6H5–CH2–CH(OH)–CH3, 1-phenylpropan-2-ol. The answer is C6H5MgBr + 2-methyloxirane.
x: Attack at the CH<sub>2</sub> of 2-phenyloxirane gives C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (OH next to the ring), and attack at the benzylic carbon gives 2-phenylpropan-1-ol; neither is the target.
Benzyl + oxirane gives C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH, a primary alcohol (3-phenylpropan-1-ol).
Methyl adds to the CH<sub>2</sub> of 2-benzyloxirane, giving C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, which has one carbon too many (1-phenylbutan-2-ol).

q: (R)-2-Methyloxirane is treated with CH3MgBr, followed by aqueous acid. What is the product?
h: Find which carbon is attacked. Are any bonds to the stereocenter broken?
w: The Grignard attacks the less hindered CH2 carbon, so no bond to the stereocenter is broken and its spatial arrangement is kept. CIP check at that carbon: before, O > CH2(ring, bonded to O) > CH3 > H; after, OH > CH2CH3 > CH3 > H. The priority order maps onto the same positions, so the label stays (R)-butan-2-ol.
x: Inversion happens only at the carbon that is attacked; here the attacked carbon (CH<sub>2</sub>) is not the stereocenter.
Racemization would need the stereocenter to become planar; no bond to it breaks in this S<sub>N</sub>2 opening.
This product would come from attack at the more hindered CH carbon, which Grignard reagents avoid.

q: (2R,3R)-2,3-Dimethyloxirane is treated with NaOCH3 in CH3OH. Which stereoisomer of 3-methoxybutan-2-ol forms?
h: The two epoxide carbons are equivalent here. One carbon is inverted and the other is untouched; then assign R/S.
w: The (R,R) epoxide has C2 symmetry, so attack at either carbon gives the same product. Methoxide attacks one carbon by SN2 and inverts it: that carbon (C3, now bearing OCH3) goes from R to S. The other carbon (C2, keeps the oxygen as OH) is untouched and stays R. Product: (2R,3S)-3-methoxybutan-2-ol as a single enantiomer (assignments checked with CIP software).
x: This is the enantiomer; it would come from the (S,S) epoxide.
Both centers R would mean retention at the attacked carbon; SN2 opening inverts it.
Inverting both centers would need both C–O bonds to break; only one carbon is attacked.

q: With NaOH, trans-2-chlorocyclohexan-1-ol rapidly forms cyclohexene oxide, but the cis isomer does not form an epoxide. What is the best explanation?
c: Ring closure is an internal SN2 that needs O− anti to Cl (both axial); only the trans isomer can reach that geometry
The cis isomer would have to give a trans-fused epoxide, which is too strained to form
The cis alcohol is much less acidic, so NaOH cannot form its alkoxide
The trans isomer reacts by E2, which needs an anti-periplanar H that the cis isomer lacks
h: Epoxide closure from a halohydrin is a back-side displacement. Where must the nucleophile sit relative to the leaving group?
w: The alkoxide closes the ring by intramolecular SN2, so it must approach the C–Cl carbon from the back side, anti to Cl. In the trans isomer a ring flip puts OH and Cl trans-diaxial, perfectly anti. In the cis isomer O and Cl are on the same face, so back-side attack is impossible. Only the trans isomer can place O− anti to Cl.
x: Both isomers would give the same cis-fused cyclohexene oxide if they could close; the problem is the approach geometry, not product strain.
Cis and trans chlorohydrins have very similar acidities; both are deprotonated by NaOH.
Epoxide formation is a substitution by oxygen, not an elimination of H and Cl.

q:
Rank these compounds from least acidic to most acidic.
I. CH3CH2OH II. CH3CH2SH III. CF3CH2OH
h: Compare the atom carrying the negative charge first, then the inductive effect.
w: Ethanol (pKa ≈ 16) is least acidic. Three fluorines pull electron density away inductively and stabilize CF3CH2O− (pKa ≈ 12.4). Ethanethiol is most acidic (pKa ≈ 10.6) because the charge sits on the larger, more polarizable sulfur atom, and the weaker S–H bond breaks more easily; going down a group outweighs the inductive effect here. Order: I < III < II.
x: Inductive stabilization by CF<sub>3</sub> lowers the pK<sub>a</sub> to about 12, but putting the charge on sulfur lowers it more, to about 10.6.
Fluorination makes the alcohol more acidic than ethanol, not less.
The thiol is the most acidic of the three, not the least: sulfur, being larger, holds the negative charge better than oxygen.

q: 2-Sulfanylethan-1-ol (HSCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH) is treated with one equivalent of NaOH in water, then one equivalent of CH<sub>3</sub>I. What is the major product?
h: Which proton does one equivalent of hydroxide remove? Which anion is the better nucleophile anyway?
w: The thiol (pKa ≈ 10) is far more acidic than the alcohol (pKa ≈ 16), so one equivalent of NaOH forms the thiolate. Thiolate is also a much better nucleophile than an alcohol or alkoxide in water, because sulfur is large and polarizable. It attacks CH3I by SN2, giving 2-(methylsulfanyl)ethan-1-ol.
x: O-Methylation would need the alkoxide, but NaOH deprotonates the much more acidic SH, and S<sup>−</sup> is the better nucleophile.
Only one equivalent of CH<sub>3</sub>I is used, and the neutral OH does not react with CH<sub>3</sub>I in water.
A sulfonium salt needs a second equivalent of CH<sub>3</sub>I to alkylate the sulfide; only one is available.

q: (R)-2-Bromobutane is treated with sodium methanethiolate (CH3SNa) in DMF. What is the major product?
h: Thiolates are excellent nucleophiles but weak bases. Which pathway does that favor at a secondary carbon?
w: CH3S− is a weak base (CH3SH pKa ≈ 10) but a very strong, polarizable nucleophile, and DMF is polar aprotic. So even at a secondary carbon SN2 beats E2. Back-side attack inverts the stereocenter; S replaces Br as top priority, so the product is (S)-2-(methylsulfanyl)butane.
x: Retention would require front-side attack; SN2 gives inversion, and the S group takes Br's priority rank, so the label changes to S.
E2 to (E)-but-2-ene needs a strong base such as ethoxide; methanethiolate is too weak a base to compete with its own SN2.
Hofmann-type alkene formation needs a bulky strong base; thiolate gives substitution.

q: What is the product when ethanethiol is treated with I<sub>2</sub> (a mild oxidant) in the presence of a weak base?
h: Mild oxidation of thiols forms an S–S bond.
w: Two thiol molecules are oxidized by I2, each losing an H, and their sulfur atoms join: 2 RSH → RS–SR + 2 HI. The product is diethyl disulfide. This is the same S–S bond that links cysteine residues in proteins.
x: A sulfide (thioether) has one sulfur bonded to two carbons; forming it would need an alkylation, not an oxidation.
Sulfonic acids need strong oxidants such as HNO<sub>3</sub> or KMnO<sub>4</sub>; I<sub>2</sub> stops at the disulfide.
Iodine does not replace the SH group; the thiol is oxidized at sulfur, not substituted at carbon.

q: The disulfide bond in cystine is cleaved by excess 2-mercaptoethanol (or by Zn/HCl) to give two cysteine molecules. Which statement about the sulfur atoms is correct?
c: Their oxidation state does not change; the S–S bond is hydrolyzed
h: Count each sulfur's bonds: S–S counts as zero; S is slightly more electronegative than C and more than H.
w: In the disulfide each S has one bond to C (S is assigned that electron pair: −1) and one bond to S (0), so each S is −1. In the thiol each S has a bond to C (−1) and a bond to H (−1), so S is −2. Going from disulfide to thiols, each sulfur gains a bond to H: reduction from −1 to −2. The reverse (thiols → disulfide) is an oxidation.
x: That is the reverse reaction, thiol to disulfide; breaking the S–S bond and adding H is a reduction.
The disulfide sulfur is −1, not 0, because each sulfur is also bonded to a carbon.
Each S gains an S–H bond in place of an S–S bond, so the oxidation state changes; water does not cleave disulfides.

q: Methyl phenyl sulfide is treated with excess H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> in acetic acid with heating. What is the final product?
h: Each oxidation adds one oxygen to sulfur. How many times can a sulfide sulfur be oxidized without breaking C–S bonds?
w: Sulfides are oxidized at sulfur in two steps: sulfide → sulfoxide (one O) → sulfone (two O). One equivalent of a mild oxidant (NaIO4, or 1 equiv H2O2 at low temperature) stops at the sulfoxide; excess oxidant with heat continues to the sulfone, methyl phenyl sulfone. The C–S bonds are kept.
x: The sulfoxide is the intermediate; with excess H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> and heat it is oxidized again to the sulfone.
A sulfonic acid would require breaking the S–CH<sub>3</sub> bond; peroxide oxidation adds O to S and leaves both C–S bonds.
Oxidation adds oxygen to sulfur; it does not replace sulfur by oxygen.

q: Which compound is chiral and can be isolated as a single enantiomer at room temperature?
h: A sulfoxide sulfur is pyramidal with a lone pair as its fourth "group". Look for four different groups.
w: The sulfoxide sulfur is tetrahedral: O, two carbon groups and a lone pair. Its pyramidal inversion is slow at room temperature (barrier about 160 kJ/mol), so a sulfoxide with two different carbon groups is a stable stereocenter. Methyl phenyl sulfoxide has O, CH3, C6H5 and a lone pair, so it is chiral and resolvable.
x: A sulfone has two identical oxygens on sulfur, so the sulfur is not a stereocenter.
Diphenyl sulfoxide has two identical phenyl groups, so it has a mirror plane and is achiral.
DMSO has two identical methyl groups, so it is achiral.

q: Which compound reacts with CH<sub>3</sub>I at room temperature to give a stable, isolable salt?
h: Compare how nucleophilic, and how basic, sulfur and oxygen lone pairs are.
w: Divalent sulfur is large and polarizable, so sulfides are good nucleophiles even though they are weak bases. Dimethyl sulfide attacks CH3I by SN2 to give trimethylsulfonium iodide, (CH3)3S+ I−, a stable salt. Ethers are poor nucleophiles, and trialkyloxonium ions are too reactive to form this way. The answer is dimethyl sulfide.
x: Dimethyl ether's oxygen is a poor nucleophile; a trimethyloxonium salt does not form from CH<sub>3</sub>I.
Diethyl ether is a common solvent for reactions of alkyl halides precisely because it does not react with them.
THF's oxygen lone pairs coordinate to metals (as in Grignard reagents), but THF is not nucleophilic enough to be alkylated by CH<sub>3</sub>I.

q: Which sequence converts (R)-butan-2-ol into (R)-2-methoxybutane?
h: Decide which C–O bond must stay intact to keep the configuration.
w: To keep the configuration, the C–O bond at the stereocenter must not break. NaH forms the alkoxide (the stereocenter is untouched), and the alkoxide attacks CH3I by SN2 at the methyl carbon. The new bond is O–CH3, so the stereocenter keeps its arrangement: 1. NaH 2. CH3I gives (R)-2-methoxybutane (CIP label confirmed).
x: Tosylation keeps the configuration, but methoxide then displaces OTs by SN2 at the stereocenter, giving (S)-2-methoxybutane (plus some E2 alkene).
Acid with a secondary alcohol gives elimination and S<sub>N</sub>1 mixtures that lose the stereochemistry; it is not a clean route to one enantiomer of the ether.
A neutral alcohol reacts very slowly with CH<sub>3</sub>I; the alkoxide must be formed first, so the order of steps matters.

q: Which sequence converts cyclohexene into the product shown (racemic; one enantiomer drawn)?
h: The target has two oxygens on adjacent carbons, trans. Which route adds two oxygens anti?
w: Epoxidation adds one oxygen across the double bond. Ethoxide then opens the epoxide by back-side SN2, placing OCH2CH3 trans to the alkoxide, which ethanol protonates. The sequence 1. mCPBA 2. NaOCH2CH3, CH3CH2OH gives trans-2-ethoxycyclohexan-1-ol.
x: OsO4 adds both OH groups syn, so this route gives the cis ether-alcohol (and mixtures from the diol).
Alkoxymercuration adds only one oxygen (ethoxycyclohexane); the product needs an OH on the next carbon.
Hydroboration–oxidation adds only one OH, so this sequence gives ethoxycyclohexane with no second oxygen.

q: Epoxides are opened by hydroxide or alkoxides under mild conditions, while diethyl ether is inert to them. What is the main reason?
c: The three-membered ring is strained, and opening it releases about 110 kJ/mol of ring strain
Epoxide carbons are sp<sup>2</sup> hybridized, like a carbonyl carbon
The epoxide oxygen carries a formal positive charge
Epoxides are aromatic, and opening the ring relieves antiaromatic strain
h: Compare the C–O–C bond angle in an epoxide with the normal tetrahedral angle.
w: In an epoxide the ring bond angles are about 60°, far from 109.5°, so the ring holds roughly 110 kJ/mol of angle and torsional strain. Opening the ring releases that strain, which makes the alkoxide leaving group acceptable. An acyclic ether has no such driving force. Answer: ring strain.
x: Epoxide carbons are sp<sup>3</sup>; they have no π bond.
A neutral epoxide oxygen has two bonds and two lone pairs, so its formal charge is zero.
An epoxide has no π electrons and cannot be aromatic or antiaromatic.
